solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Male warmonger carrying a fighting-axe (8)

indicators.note: whatever carries something holds it, so the male and the warmonger hold the A between them

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
a hawk is a politician keen on war

annotation.surface: A belligerent man goes about armed with a battle-axe.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one man carrying a weapon, but Male and warmonger are separate pieces that hold the A between them.
annotation.definitionFit: A tomahawk is the light axe of North American peoples, used in fighting.

clue.text: Intruder very dated in French resistance (10)

blocks.note: passé is French for past it, dated
tells you to put very and dated into French
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

annotation.surface: Someone recalls the long-ago days of the French Resistance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'French resistance' wants to be one phrase, the wartime underground, but French belongs with very and dated, and resistance stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A trespasser is someone who intrudes on land without right.

clue.text: Bad name for a soft earthy substance (3)

blocks.note: from the idiom saying someone's name is in disgrace

annotation.surface: Some soft, earthy material has been given an unflattering label.
annotation.walkthrough: The idiom 'your name is mud' means you are in disgrace, so mud itself stands for a bad name.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description of wet soil for one sense; the other is the idiom 'his name is mud', said of someone in disgrace.

clue.text: Musical security device protecting the locks? (7)

blocks.note: a PIN is the security number for a bank card

annotation.surface: A tuneful gadget keeps the locks on a door safe.
annotation.walkthrough: Locks look like door locks guarded by a security device, but they are locks of hair, which a hairpin holds in place.
annotation.definitionFit: A hairpin keeps locks of hair in place, so it protects the locks; the question mark flags the pun.

clue.text: Player on pitch, one hanging on to gate (12)

blocks.note: a wicket is a small gate
a keeper is one who holds on to something

annotation.surface: A footballer leans on the gate at the edge of the pitch.
annotation.walkthrough: The wicketkeeper is the cricket fielder who crouches behind the batsman's stumps; the pieces come in reverse clue order.
annotation.definitionFit: The wicketkeeper is one of the cricket team out on the pitch.

clue.text: Parisian gangster quickly seizing hostage at the outset (6)

indicators.note: to seize is to grab and hold, so APACE takes hold of the H
the outset is the start, so take the first letter of hostage

annotation.surface: A Paris hoodlum moves fast to grab a hostage at the start of a raid.
annotation.walkthrough: Apache was the early-1900s name for a Paris street ruffian, borrowed from the Native American people.
annotation.definitionFit: An apache was a violent Parisian street criminal.

clue.text: Sound out head of maths about ultimately equivocal sum? (7)

indicators.note: the head is the top, so take the first letter of maths
about means around, so PROBE and M go around the L
ultimately means in the end, so take the last letter of equivocal

blocks.note: to probe is to sound out

annotation.surface: Someone tests the senior maths teacher on an ambiguous calculation.
annotation.walkthrough: Head of maths reads as a senior teacher, but it is only an M, and 'sum' with a question mark is a classroom exercise, not addition.
annotation.definitionFit: A sum set in class is a problem; the question mark admits a sum is only one kind.

clue.text: Observation about trick over small storage area (11)

indicators.note: about means around, so COMMENT goes around the reversed trick
something turned over faces the other way, so TRAP runs backwards

annotation.surface: Someone remarks on a scam involving a little storeroom.
annotation.walkthrough: Small wants to be S, but it belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A compartment is a small separate space for storing things.

clue.text: Predatory type seen in Inverness (4)

indicators.note: the answer can be seen inside the next word

blocks.note: letters three to six of the city's name

annotation.surface: A predator has been spotted in the Scottish Highland city.
annotation.walkthrough: The erne, the white-tailed sea eagle, is a crossword regular; it was reintroduced to Scotland, so the surface is apt.
annotation.definitionFit: An erne is a sea eagle, a bird of prey.

clue.text: Scot’s weird longing to follow presbyter, not English (8)

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so ITCH comes after the presbyter
'not English' means without English, so the E is taken out

blocks.note: an elder is a presbyter; drop E for English

annotation.surface: A Scotsman has a strange urge to trail after a church elder.
annotation.walkthrough: A presbyter is a church elder; which E goes does not matter, since ELDER without either gives ELDR.
annotation.definitionFit: Eldritch is a Scottish word for weird or eerie.

clue.text: Archer’s old wife meeting maiden in bar (6)

indicators.note: things that meet come together, so O and W sit right next to M
the O, W and M go inside BAN

blocks.note: M for maiden, an over with no runs in cricket scoring

annotation.surface: In The Archers radio soap, an old wife meets a young woman in the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: Archer's with a capital suggests the BBC soap The Archers, but it is just the definition plus 'is', and bar is not the pub but a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Bowman is the older plain-English word for an archer, one who shoots with a bow.

clue.text: Clinically carving up Italy, visit in any case (12)

indicators.note: cutting Italy up rearranges its letters
ANY is the case that holds the rest

blocks.note: to call on is to visit

annotation.surface: An invading power coldly divides up Italy, dropping in anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In any case' reads as a throwaway 'anyway', which is why it slips past as filler; here the word any is a literal case holding everything else.
annotation.definitionFit: Doing something clinically means doing it analytically, coolly and without emotion.

clue.text: Hear a pal in rap, changing bits and pieces (13)

indicators.note: the letters change places

annotation.surface: You listen to a friend performing in a rap, switching between different parts.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder reads as a sentence about music, which hides the fact that it is exactly thirteen letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Paraphernalia are miscellaneous belongings or bits of equipment.

clue.text: Naval officer adapted drama, initially recasting Ariel (4,7)

indicators.note: the letters of drama are adapted
takes the first letter of recasting
casting Ariel again rearranges the name

annotation.surface: A sailor stages a new version of a play and first replaces the actor playing Ariel, the spirit in The Tempest.
annotation.walkthrough: Recasting does double work: its R joins the fodder, and the word itself tells you to shuffle Ariel.
annotation.definitionFit: A rank title: the rear admiral is the lowest of the navy's admirals, so a naval officer by example.

clue.text: Woollen cloth Irish plunged in Kentucky lake (10)

indicators.note: ERSE is dropped inside KY

blocks.note: Erse is the Irish Gaelic language

annotation.surface: A bolt of wool from Ireland has been thrown into a lake in Kentucky.
annotation.walkthrough: An obscure word, so trust the pieces: the Irish plunges into the state, not the lake.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialist textile name: kerseymere is a fine twilled cloth, a variant of kersey, so woollen cloth is its category.

clue.text: Fellow hiding current shame (5)

indicators.note: STAN hides the I inside it

blocks.note: Stan is a man's name, any fellow
I is the symbol for electric current

annotation.surface: A man conceals something he is currently ashamed of.
annotation.walkthrough: Fellow suggests F or a college don, but here it is just a man's name.
annotation.definitionFit: A stain on one's name is a mark of shame.

clue.text: Like Tom, confused about measure of distance (9)

indicators.note: the letters of Like Tom are muddled

annotation.surface: Like Tom, someone is puzzled about how far something is.
annotation.walkthrough: About looks like a container or reversal signal, but it is RE, tacked on the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A kilometre is a thousand metres, a unit of distance.

clue.text: Aim of Bill’s deed followed by chaps in hospital department (9)

indicators.note: what is followed has something coming after it, so the deed comes first and the chaps after
ACT and MEN go inside ENT

annotation.surface: Bill wants to be the man who does the deed and then meets his mates in a hospital ward.
annotation.walkthrough: Bill reads as a man's name because it opens the possessive; it is a parliamentary bill, whose aim is to become law.
annotation.definitionFit: A bill in parliament aims to become law, and its enactment is that goal achieved.

clue.text: Former PM endlessly surrounded by regularly stark gossip (7)

indicators.note: cuts the last letter from ATTLEE
ATTLE sits inside the other letters
takes every other letter of stark

blocks.note: Clement Attlee, British prime minister 1945-51, minus his last E

annotation.surface: A former prime minister is hemmed in by blunt rumour-mongering.
annotation.walkthrough: Stark looks like an adjective for the gossip, but regularly reduces it to two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A tattler is a gossip, someone who tells tales.

clue.text: Glorify Good Queen providing accommodation for fifty (5)

indicators.note: BESS gives the L somewhere to stay

blocks.note: Good Queen Bess was Elizabeth I's nickname

annotation.surface: Praise be to the kindly queen who put up fifty guests.
annotation.walkthrough: Good looks like G, but 'Good Queen' together is Bess, the popular name for Elizabeth I.
annotation.definitionFit: A religious sense: to bless God, as in hymns and psalms, is to praise and extol Him.

clue.text: Club employee, a lively, energetic individual! (7)

blocks.note: the doorman who keeps order at a nightclub

annotation.surface: A nightclub worker is praised as bubbly and full of beans.
annotation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal and jokey: anyone who bounces is a bouncer.
annotation.definitionFit: A bouncer is the heavy on a club's door, and also one who bounces.

clue.text: Dam river in Kent perhaps, the place of one’s birth (6,7)

indicators.note: the river is placed in the county, the way a river runs through one

blocks.note: a dam is an animal's mother
Kent is an English county; perhaps marks an example

annotation.surface: A dam holds back a river somewhere in Kent, where someone was born.
annotation.walkthrough: Dam wants to be a barrage across the river, but here it is a mother, as in horse breeding.
annotation.definitionFit: Your mother country is the land you were born in.

clue.text: Birds Greek character captured in French art (4)

indicators.note: the Greek letter is held inside ES

annotation.surface: Some birds and a Greek figure appear in a French painting.
annotation.walkthrough: Art is the old verb, as in 'thou art', not painting.
annotation.definitionFit: Emus are large flightless Australian birds.

clue.text: Increasingly accepting nearly everyone’s state of mind (6)

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so MORE takes the letters in
cuts the last letter from ALL

annotation.surface: Nearly everyone is growing more tolerant in their outlook.
annotation.walkthrough: Accepting reads as tolerant, an attitude that fits the state of mind, but it only means holding.
annotation.definitionFit: Morale is the confidence and spirit of a person or group.

clue.text: Obstruction demanded to protect part of canal (8)

indicators.note: BADE wraps around LOCK to guard it

blocks.note: a lock is a section of canal with gates

annotation.surface: Guards were ordered to defend a canal lock against a barricade.
annotation.walkthrough: Demanded is the old past tense bade, which few solvers reach for first.
annotation.definitionFit: A military sense: a blockade cuts off a port or city, an obstruction on a large scale.

clue.text: Some article — extremely newsy! (3)

indicators.note: takes the letters at the extremes of newsy

blocks.note: first and last letters of newsy

annotation.surface: A newspaper piece is packed with news.
annotation.walkthrough: Some leads the clue and looks like a hidden-word signal, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Have you any?' and 'have you some?' mean the same.

clue.text: Income, sad to say, taken back by railway (6)

indicators.note: something taken back returns the way it came, so ALAS runs backwards

annotation.surface: Sadly, someone's pay has been cut by the rail company.
annotation.walkthrough: Taken back reads as reclaimed money, but it only reverses ALAS.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym narrowed: a salary is the fixed income paid for a job, one kind of income.

clue.text: Poet’s mature relationship with nature, for example (3,5)

definitions.text: Poet’s mature relationship with nature, for example

blocks.note: reads as a poet's grown-up bond, but mature is just a word the poet might use at a line's end
nature is the partner word: the endings are spelt alike but sound different

annotation.surface: A poet has grown into a grown-up bond with the natural world.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like Wordsworth's love of nature, but mature and nature are the pair: spelt alike at the end, pronounced differently.
annotation.definitionFit: An eye rhyme is a pair of words that match in spelling but not in sound.
